children: On the eve of its developer conference, OpenAI scrapped the release of its most advanced artificial intelligence model due to safety concerns.

According to a report from The Wall Street Journal, OpenAI isn't moving ahead with the release of its GPT-6.1 Astra, which was initially slated to be announced in the coming days or weeks with a potential October debut.
The company chose not to release the model after concerns raised by researchers during internal testing, the report states. OpenAI is instead focusing on improving the safety of future models.
Barron's has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

Conversations surrounding the threats AI could pose to society have garnered a lot of attention following news that OpenAI's models took "dangerous actions that no human directed," to breach the systems of Hugging Face, another AI company.

On Friday, OpenAI said it halted the training of its latest AI models and would resume training them "only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place."
It is highly expected that OpenAI will address cybersecurity concerns during the company's annual developer conference on Tuesday.

DevDay is an annual event where the company announces new updates it plans to launch. Last year's DevDay included the introduction of apps in ChatGPT, which allows users to interact with external apps directly in the chatbot.

The 2026 DevDay will kick off with a keynote by CEO Sam Altman at 1 p.m. ET. OpenAI software engineer Tibo Sottiaux said in a post on X the conference will have "some really fun stuff, but also many many things that should change the way you work."
The internet has been buzzing about expected announcements during the keynote.

According to a Sept. 26 report from TestingCatalog, OpenAI could showcase an always-on assistant, expected to be called "O," that's designed to run in the background and complete tasks such as managing emails and other workflows. OpenAI didn't respond to a Barron's request for comment on the report.

Wall Street has been paying close attention to AI agents and their capabilities following Meta Platforms' launch of Muse earlier this month. Muse is a personal AI assistant that can complete tasks for a user from a simple prompt. Potential tasks include looking through user emails to find subscriptions and cancel them, or searching for a cheaper car insurance quote.
Muse's rollout has so far been successful, and experts widely believe more agents should be coming soon from fellow AI labs.
"Every AI company is going to launch or relaunch memory intensive assistants for the next 2 years," wrote Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes on Monday.

DevDay gives OpenAI an opportunity to show that it is well positioned to compete in the agentic race, while also giving it a platform to speak directly to how it is combating cyber threats posed by highly-capable AI models.
